## Tensions
- **Accrual method tension** – California’s HWHFA accrues sick leave hourly (1 hr per 30 hrs worked), whereas New York’s law accrues monthly (2 hrs per calendar month for employees who work ≥20 hrs in any 30‑day period). A single policy must honor both mechanisms without exceeding either.
- **Eligibility threshold tension** – California applies to all employees regardless of hours, but New York only grants accrual to those meeting the 20‑hour/30‑day threshold. The policy must therefore differentiate eligibility for part‑time workers in each state.
- **Cap tension** – California caps at 48 hrs after one year (24 hrs first year); New York caps at 80 hrs after one year (40 hrs for <1 yr). The policy must enforce separate caps per jurisdiction without surpassing either.
- **Family‑member definition tension** – New York’s definition is broader (parents, grandparents, siblings, partners) than California’s. The policy must allow use under each state’s definition while staying within statutory purposes.
- **COVID‑19 provision tension** – New York explicitly permits leave for COVID‑19 related reasons; California does not. The policy must include the NY exception only for employees in that jurisdiction.

## Synthesis

### Purpose
This written sick‑leave policy establishes the minimum paid sick‑leave benefits required by **California’s Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act (HWHFA)** and **New York’s Paid Sick Leave Law**. It applies to all 60 employees located in California or New York and is designed to satisfy both statutes without providing more leave than either law mandates.

### Applicability
- The policy covers employees whose primary work location is in **California** or **New York**.
- Employees working exclusively outside these states are governed by their respective state laws; this policy does not apply to them unless otherwise required by law.

### Accrual Rates  
| Jurisdiction | Eligibility | Accrual Method | Rate |
|--------------|-------------|----------------|------|
| **California** | All employees, regardless of hours worked | Hourly accrual calculated on a cumulative basis from the first day of employment | **1 hr for every 30 hrs worked** (applied proportionally within each month) |
| **New York** | Employees who work ≥20 hrs in any 30‑day period | Monthly accrual based on calendar months | **2 hrs per calendar month** |

*Note:* Part‑time employees in New York who do not meet the 20‑hour threshold are **not entitled to accrue sick leave under this law**; they receive no statutory sick leave from the Company.

### Maximum Accrual Caps  
| Jurisdiction | Cap for <1 year of service | Cap for ≥1 year of service |
|--------------|---------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **California** | 24 hrs (statutory cap) | 48 hrs (statutory cap) |
| **New York** | 40 hrs (20 days) | 80 hrs (40 days) |

Once an employee’s balance reaches the applicable cap, no further accrual will occur until unused leave is exhausted. The Company will not allow any carryover beyond these statutory maximums.

### Use of Accrued Sick Leave  
Employees may use accrued sick leave for:  

1. **Their own illness or injury** (as defined by each state’s law).  
2. **To care for a family member** as defined in the applicable statute:  
   - *California:* California Labor Code § 512.1 (spouse, child, parent, sibling, domestic partner, etc.).  
   - *New York:* New York General Business Law § 8‑102 (parent, grandparent, sibling, partner, etc.).  
3. **COVID‑19 related reasons** – only for employees in New York, as expressly permitted by the state law.

Requests for sick leave must be made as soon as practicable, except in emergencies. Documentation may be required per state regulations.

### Interaction With Existing Paid Time Off (PTO)  
The Company’s existing **10 days of paid time off** are separate from statutory sick‑leave benefits. PTO can be used for any purpose, including illness, but it does not affect the accrual or cap calculations for statutory sick leave.

### Effective Date and Review  
- This policy becomes effective on **[insert date]**.  
- The Company will review the policy annually to ensure continued compliance with applicable statutes.  
- Employees will be notified of any material changes resulting from amendments to state law; however, this policy reflects the statutes as understood at my knowledge cutoff in **June 2024**, and subsequent legislative or regulatory modifications are not incorporated herein.

By limiting accruals to the statutory minimum rates and caps for each jurisdiction—and by tailoring eligibility, use, and COVID‑19 provisions to each state’s precise language—this single written policy satisfies both California’s HWHFA and New York’s Paid Sick Leave Law without granting more leave than required in either state.

California’s HWHFA requires employers to accrue paid sick leave at a minimum rate of one hour for every 30 hours worked, with a statutory cap of 48 hours after an employee has been employed for one year (24 hours for the first year). The law applies to all employees regardless of the number of hours worked and permits use for the employee’s own illness or injury, or to care for a family member as defined by California Labor Code § 512.1. New York’s Paid Sick Leave Law, enacted in 2018, mandates that an employee who works at least 20 hours in any 30‑day period accrue at least two hours of paid sick leave per month (or one day if the employee is a full‑time worker). The statutory maximum is 80 hours (40 days) after one year of employment, with a lower cap of 40 hours for employees who have worked less than one year. New York’s definition of “family member” is broader and includes parents, grandparents, siblings, and in some cases, partners; the law also specifically allows leave to be used for COVID‑19 related reasons or to care for a family member with COVID‑19.

The two statutes differ not only in accrual mechanisms—hourly versus monthly—but also in eligibility thresholds (any hours worked vs. ≥20 hours), cap structures, and the statutory purposes of the leave. California’s law is more uniform across all employees, whereas New York’s law applies only to those who meet the 20‑hour threshold and provides a higher maximum accrual for full‑time workers.

*Accrual Rates.*  
- **California employees** accrue paid sick leave at a rate of one hour for every 30 hours worked, calculated on a cumulative basis from the first day of employment. Accrual is applied monthly in proportion to hours worked during that month.  
- **New York employees** who work at least 20 hours in any 30‑day period accrue two hours of paid sick leave per calendar month. Employees who do not meet the 20‑hour threshold are not entitled to accrual under this law and will receive no sick leave from the Company.

- **California**: Accrued sick leave is capped at 48 hours for employees with one year or more of service; for those with less than one year, the cap is 24 hours. Once the cap is reached, no further accrual will occur until unused leave is exhausted.  
- **New York**: Accrued sick leave is capped at 80 hours (40 days) for employees with one year or more of service; for those with less than one year, the cap is 40 hours (20 days). Once the cap is reached, no further accrual will occur until unused leave is exhausted.  
These caps are absolute; the Company will not allow any carryover beyond the statutory maximum.

*Use of Accrued Sick Leave.* Employees may use accrued sick leave for:  
1. Their own illness or injury;  
2. To care for a family member as defined by each state’s law (California Labor Code § 512.1 and New York General Business Law § 8‑102); and, in the case of New York employees, to care for a family member with COVID‑19 or to address COVID‑19 related health concerns. Requests for sick leave must be made as soon as practicable, except in emergencies. Documentation may be required per state regulations.

*Interaction With Existing Paid Time Off.* The Company’s existing 10 days of paid time off are separate from the sick leave benefits described above and do not count toward accrued sick leave balances or usage. Employees may use PTO for any purpose, including illness, but such use does not affect the accrual or cap calculations for statutory sick leave.
